claims.text: Depression rates in children born between 1965 and 1996 showed no effect of year of birth.
The overall prevalence estimate of depression for children under age 13 is 2.8%.
The overall prevalence estimate of depression for adolescents aged 13 to 18 is 5.6%.
The overall prevalence estimate of depression for girls aged 13 to 18 is 5.9%.
The overall prevalence estimate of depression for boys aged 13 to 18 is 4.6%.
There is no evidence for an increased prevalence of child or adolescent depression over the past 30 years when concurrent assessment is used.

evidence.description: Rates of depression showed no effect of year of birth in a meta-analysis of close to 60,000 observations.
The overall prevalence estimates were: under 13, 2.8% (standard error .5%).
The overall prevalence estimates were: 13-18, 5.6% (standard error .3%).
The overall prevalence estimates were: 13-18 girls: 5.9% (standard error .3%).
The overall prevalence estimates were: 13-18 boys: 4.6% (standard error .3%).
When concurrent assessment rather than retrospective recall is used, there is no evidence for an increased prevalence of child or adolescent depression over the past 30 years.

methodologies.name: Epidemiologic Meta-Analysis
methodologies.description: Systematic review and meta-analysis of epidemiologic studies using structured diagnostic interviews to assess formal depression diagnoses on representative population samples, controlling for age, sex, sample size, taxonomy, measurement instrument, and interview time-frame.
datasets: Close to 60,000 observations on children born between 1965 and 1996
conditions: Representative population samples up to age 18

limitations.text: Prior claims of an epidemic relied on retrospective recall by successive birth cohorts of adults.
Child and adolescent depression was long under-diagnosed by clinicians in past practice.
